extracted.intended_audience: policy analysts, regulatory economists, legal practitioners, employers, and public commenters on the FTC non-compete rule
extracted.subtask_description: Economic and regulatory-analysis criteria and assumptions the FTC used to evaluate the benefits, costs, transfers, and distributional effects of its final non-compete rule, including measurement choices, data sources, and sensitivity analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Earnings
rubrics_metrics.description: Estimated ten-year present discounted value of increased worker earnings is $400–$488 billion; primary percent increase in workers' earnings estimated at 0.86%; sensitivity analyses yield larger estimates (e.g., 3.2% under full extrapolation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission treats increases in earnings as arising from more efficient matching and increased bargaining power. It acknowledges that part of the earnings effect represents transfers from firms to workers and that the literature does not separate transfers from productivity benefits. Calculation follows: Increase in worker earnings = (% Increase in Earnings caused by the change in enforceability of non-competes) * (Total Affected Earnings). Total affected annual earnings used: $6.2 trillion (primary) and $7.3 trillion (full extrapolation). Ten-year PDVs discounted at 2%, 3%, and 7% are reported.

rubrics_metrics.name: Innovation (patenting activity as proxy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Innovation measured in part by patenting: annual patent counts estimated to rise by 3,111–5,337 in year one and 31,110–53,372 in year ten; annual R&D spending estimated to fall by $0–$47 billion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission acknowledges that patenting does not capture the full social value of innovation but treats patent counts as a useful proxy. It stops short of monetizing the social value of patents because such estimates are not available, though it discusses private-value estimates in the literature and uses sensitivity/break-even reasoning involving assumed social patent values elsewhere in the analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prices
rubrics_metrics.description: Partially quantified: estimated ten-year present discounted value of decreases in spending on physician and clinical services is $74–$194 billion; other sectors' price effects may exist but are not fully quantified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Price changes can be a mix of transfers (from firms to consumers) and benefits (due to increased competition) and may affect quantity, choice, and quality. The literature has not quantified price effects outside physician/clinical services; the Commission reports partial quantification and discusses uncertainty about the split between transfers and benefits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investment in human capital
rubrics_metrics.description: Monetized range for ten-year present discounted value of net effect on human capital investment: benefit of $32 billion to a cost of $41 billion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uncertainty arises from whether observed decreases in training reflect reductions in advanced training (a potential societal cost) or reductions in core training (an efficiency gain). Evidence does not allow distinguishing core versus advanced training effects. The Commission treats this range as reflecting that ambiguity and reports it as monetized with caveats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal and administrative costs
rubrics_metrics.description: One-time legal and administrative compliance costs estimated at $2.1–$3.7 billion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analysis accounts for simplified notice processes, model safe-harbor notice language, and the allowance to use last known addresses (mail or electronic) which reduce employer burdens. Sensitivity analyses consider higher attorney cost assumptions and different time assumptions for employer compliance activities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Litigation effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Not quantified or monetized: litigation costs may increase or decrease; effects on litigation may represent either costs or benefits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission recognizes trade secret and post-employment restriction litigation can be costly (commenters cited $550k–$7.4M ranges), but finds no evidence that such litigation will increase because of the final rule. It expects decreased non‑compete litigation due to a clear, bright-line Federal standard may offset any increases, but data on frequencies are lacking, so the effect remains unquantified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Firm expansion and formation
rubrics_metrics.description: Quantified: final rule estimated to increase new firm formation by 2.7–3.2% and decrease capital investment at incumbent firms by 0–7.9%.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These effects represent a shift in productive capacity from incumbent firms to new firms; new firm formation is generally a benefit but may crowd out incumbents, making this a distributional (not purely positive) effect. The Commission reports these effects and discusses implications for net welfare.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distributional effects on workers
rubrics_metrics.description: Not quantified or monetized: the rule may reduce gender and racial earnings gaps, disproportionately encourage entrepreneurship among women, and mitigate legal uncertainty for workers, especially lower-paid workers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission flags these as important distributional outcomes and does not monetize them, instead describing how benefits and costs may be unevenly distributed across demographic groups and occupations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Labor mobility and turnover costs
rubrics_metrics.description: Partially monetized: estimated increase in turnover costs for firms using non-competes is bounded at no more than $131 per worker with a non-compete; some turnover-related savings for other firms are not monetized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Labor mobility effects include both increased turnover costs for some firms and hiring-cost savings for others; the Commission treats net effects as ambiguous and likely distributional. The $131 per-worker estimate is an upper bound capturing multiple components (investment in human capital, hiring, lost productivity) and is likely conservative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coverage rate estimation
rubrics_metrics.description: Final rule likely to cover 80% of the private U.S. workforce (estimate based on ACS microdata 2017–2021).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coverage rate estimated by classifying workers according to (1) government employment, (2) nonprofit status, and (3) industry/capacity likely outside FTC jurisdiction (NAICS). Residents of four States (California, Minnesota, North Dakota, Oklahoma) were excluded from the sample because these States already broadly disallow non-competes. Where ambiguity existed, the Commission overinclusive-excluded workers (e.g., classifying all nonprofits as outside coverage), producing conservative (under)estimates of coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-compete enforceability scoring system
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of a 0–1 enforceability score: 0 indicates enforceability equal to the State enforcing non-competes least (North Dakota); 1 indicates enforceability equal to the State enforcing most readily (Florida).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission gives greatest weight to studies that measure enforceability granularly (not binary) and along dimensions (e.g., employer's burden of proof, extent courts may modify contracts). The selected score varies across States and years and is used heavily to map legal changes into economic outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary assumption on magnitude of change (average yearly change = 0.081)
rubrics_metrics.description: For the primary analysis the Commission assumes the projected effects on economic outcomes equal the effects associated in the literature with an average magnitude change in the enforceability score of 0.081 (on a 0–1 scale).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This choice avoids extrapolating beyond observed empirical changes (the final rule implies a much larger change, average decrease 0.78). The Commission notes this approach may understate effects and therefore presents sensitivity analyses that extrapolate to larger enforceability changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensitivity analyses (full and partial extrapolation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two sensitivity approaches: (a) Full extrapolation assumes enforceability scores fall to zero and estimates a larger earnings effect (e.g., 3.2%); (b) Partial extrapolation scales effects to bring each State to the minimum observed enforceability score excluding States that broadly prohibit non-competes (0.53, New York).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Full extrapolation multiplies empirical-literature effects to the complete prohibition scenario; partial extrapolation applies a more moderate scaling to the New York benchmark. Sensitivity analyses are performed state-by-state rather than using a single national scaling factor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Earnings calculation formula and parameters
rubrics_metrics.description: Increase in worker earnings = (% Increase in Earnings caused by the change in enforceability) * (Total Affected Earnings). Primary parameter values: % effect 0.86%, total affected annual earnings $6.2 trillion; full extrapolation uses 3.2% and $7.3 trillion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission describes the arithmetic and data sources for the inputs, explains why different totals are used in different sensitivity analyses, and reports resulting annual and ten-year PDV estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conservative assumptions and break-even analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission uses conservative assumptions (e.g., presuming monetizable benefits are low and costs are on the high end) and conducts break-even exercises (e.g., if only 5.5% of estimated $400–$488 billion earnings increase represents productivity, benefits outweigh costs; or social value of a patent must be at least $297,144 for monetizable benefits to exceed monetized costs under certain assumptions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These analyses intentionally understate benefits and overstate costs to show the rule is net beneficial even under conservative parameter choices. The Commission also notes private patent-value estimates in the literature (up to $32 million) to contextualize conservatism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliance on empirical literature and study selection criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Priority given to empirical studies that measure enforceability granularly (e.g., integer scales) and capture multiple dimensions relevant to enforceability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission explains that studies with finer-grained enforceability measures better support mapping legal changes to economic outcomes, and that much of the regulatory analysis relies on studies using an enforceability score that varies across State and year.

rubrics_metrics.name: Baseline and jurisdictional classification caveats
rubrics_metrics.description: Baseline conditions constructed using ACS data with acknowledged imperfections: FTC jurisdiction does not map perfectly to ACS classifications, and some NAICS categories include subsets that may be outside FTC jurisdiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When ambiguity arose, the Commission erred on excluding workers from coverage (making the coverage estimate conservative). The analysis documents these mapping issues and the direction of bias introduced by conservative choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of senior executives
rubrics_metrics.description: Existing non-competes with senior executives may remain in effect; for senior executives the rule prohibits new non-competes entered into after the effective date (enforcement differs by time of agreement).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission notes that differential treatment of senior executives likely affects some costs and benefits temporarily (senior executives will eventually move jobs), but precise quantitative effects are not separately monetized. This difference is highlighted throughout the analysis as it may bias certain estimates temporarily.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of deferred compensation, bonuses, severance, and training
rubrics_metrics.description: Deferred compensation and structured payments may remain permissible if they do not meet the definition of 'non-compete clause'; evidence suggests worker-sponsored training is unaffected by non-compete enforceability; effect on firm-sponsored training is ambiguous between core vs advanced training.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission explains that many incentive payments have contingencies other than non-competes and likely retain employer value. For training, because empirical evidence doesn't distinguish core from advanced training, the Commission treats decreases in training as potentially either net benefits (if core falls) or net costs (if advanced falls), and discusses this ambiguity in monetization of human capital effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Present value discounting
rubrics_metrics.description: Ten-year present values are calculated using discount rates of 2%, 3%, and 7%.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All monetized multi-year estimates (earnings, prices, legal/admin costs, investment in human capital) are reported as PDVs using these three discount rates to show sensitivity to discounting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attorney cost sensitivity (implementation cost)
rubrics_metrics.description: Primary estimate for average hourly productivity of an attorney is $134.62 (BLS data); sensitivity uses outside-counsel rate of $483 per hour (tenth-year attorney) to examine higher-cost compliance scenarios.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission replaces the primary attorney-hour cost with a higher outside-counsel rate in a sensitivity analysis and conducts a separate sensitivity varying time employers spend updating contracts to estimate a range of one-time legal/administrative costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice process simplification and model safe harbor
rubrics_metrics.description: Final rule provides model safe-harbor notice language and allows use of last known address, mail or electronic, to simplify compliance and reduce notice-related costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These procedural measures are cited as likely to reduce compliance costs and litigation costs over whether notices were properly provided; they factor into the Commission's lower-bound cost estimates for implementation.
